stops.name: Edinburgh Castle
stops.en: Iconic fortress perched magnificently on a volcanic rock above the city. The castle has been continuously used for 1100 years and is kept in excellent condition; it's still the ceremonial headquarters of the army in Scotland. Highlights include the Great Hall, the Honours of Scotland (the Scottish Crown Jewels), the War Museum and the 12th century St Margaret's Chapel. The One O'Clock Gun is fired

stops.name: Holyrood Palace
stops.en: The Palace is a royal residence, closed when the king is here for a week in July and for similar state occasions. It's been repeatedly smashed up and rebuilt, and the present building is mostly from the 1670s. Highlights are the grand stair, state apartments, throne room, Mary Queen of Scots Chambers (where bloodstains from the murder of Rizzio are still visible), King's Gallery a sample of the ro

stops.name: Scottish National Gallery
stops.en: This holds much of Scotland's fine artwork from Renaissance to 20th century, with changing exhibitions. These rotate seasonally, so an exhibition put on for the Festival typically stays to the end of the year, allowing quieter times to view. Enter from the plaza between gallery and Royal Scottish Academy, and a basement passage connects the two exhibition spaces. The Scottish Galleries on the lowe

stops.name: Scott Monument
stops.en: Sir Walter Scott (1771-1832) re-invented Scotland. In the late Georgian era, he popularised tales of its medieval and Jacobean tumults, and created the clan tartans you buy on Princes St. This grand Gothic memorial, part cathedral part moon rocket, was completed in 1846 to dominate the east end of Princes St. It's 200 ft 6 in / 61.1 m tall, and guided tours take you up 287 steps (no lift) to the t

stops.name: National Museum of Scotland
stops.en: Superb museum of Scotland's heritage. You enter into the lofty Victorian Grand Gallery, where the millennium clock chimes on the hour. Exhibition halls cover Scottish and world history and culture, science, technology, art and design, and natural history. Dolly the sheep, the 12th-century Lewis chess pieces, and dinosaurs are some of the highlights. NMS also run the War Museum in the castle, the M

stops.name: National Library of Scotland
stops.en: A venerable reference library, which you need membership to access, but it has public exhibitions about literature. "Treasures" is its permanent exhibition. But don't stumble in here mistaking it for Central Library across the street.

stops.name: St Giles' Cathedral
stops.en: It's often called a Cathedral, but the Church of Scotland brooks no such episcopal entity, and Charles I dubbing it "cathedral" in 1633 was one reason his head was chopped off. Safer to call it "High Kirk", though they're nowadays lenient with first time offenders. The present building is from 14th century with much Victorian Gothic, notably its crowned spire. Highlight is the Chapel of the Order

stops.name: HMY Britannia
stops.en: This ship was commissioned in 1954 and was the royal transport and residence on overseas tours until 1997. She has a length of 412 ft / 126 m and oil-fired twin turbines; she was also designed to act as a hospital ship in wartime but was never so used. Symbolically her last duty was to bring home the Governor of Hong Kong after the crown colony was handed over to China, and the last scrap of Briti

stops.name: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh
stops.en: Impressive gardens with a large collection. Great place to wander around on a sunny day, or to sit and have a picnic. Highlights include the Rock Garden; the 165-m-long herbaceous border, backed by a huge, century-old beech hedge, and the Palm House, the tallest of its kind in Britain. The Palm House reopened in October 2026 after a big restoration, and you can only see it on pre-booked tours. (Ho

stops.name: Scottish National Portrait Gallery
stops.en: Completed in 1890, this is a striking red sandstone neo-Gothic building. It holds portraits of Scots from down the ages, with new faces being added all the time: Billy Connolly and Tilda Swinton mingle with Mary Queen of Scots. The entrance hall has a grand frieze of notable Scots in procession.

stops.name: Craigmillar Castle
stops.en: Extensive ruin of a medieval castle, built from the 14th century and abandoned in the 18th. Here was hatched the plot to murder Lord Darnley, the inconvenient husband of Mary Queen of Scots. He was blown up at Kirk O'Field (now the site of the university Old College) and when that didn't do the job he was smothered.

stops.name: Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art
stops.en: The original modern art gallery, established in 1960, was in the Botanic Gardens. In 1895 it moved into this neoclassical building, originally a refuge for fatherless children, and in 1999 it expanded across the road into the neoclassical orphanage now known as Modern Two. The gardens of Modern One have been sculpted. Both buildings have extensive contemporary collections and most visitors find th

stops.name: Royal Observatory
stops.en: This opened in 1896 to replace the observatory on Calton Hill in New Town (which remained active to 2009 but is now an art exhibition space). The ROE is owned by the Science and Technology Facilities Council and houses the University of Edinburgh's Institute for Astronomy. Public evenings in winter are on Tuesday (booking essential) with talks and tours of the site.

stops.name: St Mary's Cathedral
stops.en: The Roman Catholic Cathedral was established as a chapel in 1814 and became a cathedral in 1886 for the archdiocese of Edinburgh and St Andrews. It was designed by James Gillespie Graham in neo-perpendicular style and has undergone several alterations and extensions - in the 1970s the tenements that hemmed it in were demolished. There are services twice daily in English and daily in Polish.

stops.name: St Mary's Cathedral
stops.en: This stonking great neo-Gothic church was completed in 1879, designed by Sir George Gilbert Scott, with the towers added in 1917. It's the senior Episcopal church in Scotland, within the Anglican tradition of bishops (and much else) that the Presbyterians rejected. It has daily choral services: the song school (open occasionally) has stunning murals by Phoebe Anna Traquair.

stops.name: Calton Hill
stops.en: This is the stubby crag just east of Princes Street: a short stroll up it commands great views. The "National Monument", a memorial to Scots killed in the Napoleonic Wars, was an attempt to out-do the Parthenon in Athens but the money ran out with only the west facade built. Nelson's Tower was built 1807-16 in the shape of an upturned telescope in honour of the naval hero. A Time Ball on the mast

stops.name: Royal Scottish Academy
stops.en: An august neo-classical building on The Mound, fronting onto Princes St, and its main function is to be confused with the National Gallery behind. The RSA is a separate organisation promoting contemporary Scottish art. The building hosts temporary exhibitions but doesn't have a permanent display - the Academy's extensive collection is dispersed across many galleries. That might include your own ho

stops.name: Edinburgh Zoo
stops.en: The pandas have returned to China but there's still plenty here. Penguins include gentoo, rockhopper and king, most famously Major General Sir Nils Olav III, Baron of the Bouvet Islands and mascot of the Norwegian King's Guard. Budongo Trail leads through the troupe of 15 chimpanzees. The only koalas in the UK are here, and there are some beautiful tropical birds. The zoo is on the slopes of Corst

stops.name: Scottish Parliament Building
stops.en: A unique building, designed by Spanish Catalan architect Enric Miralles, completed in 2004. It's either a daring showpiece of postmodern architecture or a national embarrassment or a bit of both, time will tell. Parliament meets Tu-Th and you can watch debates from the Public Gallery, ask for tickets at reception. First Minister's Question Time is normally Th noon-12:45PM, and you need to reserve

stops.name: Edinburgh Central Mosque
stops.en: Stately mosque and minaret completed in 1998 in a modern variant of Turkish style. You can generally look in between prayer times.

stops.name: Princes Street Gardens
stops.en: The west portion fills the valley beyond the Mound, spanning the railway tracks to the foot of castle crag. The east portion is the terrace around the Scott Monument. They were laid out in the 1820s as private gardens for residents of the street: occupants of bath chairs required a medical certificate that their condition was not contagious. Their initial opening to the public was solely at Christ

stops.name: Modern Two
stops.en: Opposite side of Belford Rd has a slightly smaller collection, but enough to infuriate about one-in-five reviewers, who rage that their kids' drawings stuck on the fridge door are better. A neon sign in the garden reassures all and sundry that "There will be no miracles".

stops.name: Lauriston Castle
stops.en: This 1590s tower house was extended in the 1820s and housed a series of prosperous families. It passed into council ownership in 1926 and the interior has been preserved in its last occupants' plush Edwardian style. Visit by pre-booked guided tour. There is free entry to the gardens (daily 8AM-4:30PM), where the centrepiece is the Japanese garden. The castle is also used as an event space.

stops.name: Fettes College
stops.en: Boarding school in an impressive building in the style of a French Château by David Bryce built between 1863 and 1869. It can be seen from far away. Not open for tourists - the best view is looking through the fence from Carrington Road.

stops.name: Camera Obscura
stops.en: Over 150 years old, the Camera Obscura projects light from the top of the tower onto a large dish in a dark room below, displaying a panorama of the city. The effect still works on overcast days or at night but is best in sunlight, when you can use a sheet of paper to "pick up" people seen in the streets and have them scurry in your hand. The tower also houses a gallery of optical illusions that w

stops.name: Edinburgh Central Library
stops.en: See Edinburgh#Connect for how to access. The internet stations are in the Learning Centre, and the building houses Central Lending Library, Central Reference Library, Central Children's Library, Edinburgh and Scottish Collections, Art & Design Library and Music Library. It has a wealth of material for research such as old newspapers and maps, but births, marriages and deaths are filed at East Regi

stops.name: George IV Bridge
stops.en: This high-level road courses south from the top of High Street and spans the hollow of Grassmarket. Completed in 1836, it's lined with Victorian and modern buildings such as the two libraries. Victoria Street descends into the hollow, while Victoria Terrace is a walkway above it that loops back onto Royal Mile.

stops.name: Gladstone's Land
stops.en: Thomas Gladstone was a wealthy merchant, and in 1617 he had this house refashioned to accommodate his family and to partly rent out. A "Land" means a tall narrow townhouse from the period when Old Town was cramped and the only space for development was upwards. Typically along the Royal Mile the ground floor was shops and trade, genteel folk lived on the first and second floors, and lower-income r

stops.name: Surgeons' Hall Museums
stops.en: The permanent exhibitions are the Pathology Museum, the History of Surgery and the Dental Museum. Not suitable for children under 10 as the exhibits include human remains.

stops.name: Kirk of the Canongate
stops.en: In 1687 James VII (II of England) chucked the Protestants out of Holyrood to convert it to a royal Roman Catholic chapel, the sort of behaviour that got him ousted from the monarchy the following year. The congregation moved to Infirmary St then to this building on its completion in 1691. From 1952 Queen Elizabeth II regularly attended when at Holyrood, and in 2011 her granddaughter Zara Phillips

stops.name: Old Calton Burial Ground
stops.en: Atmospheric Georgian graves, memorials, and funerary ornaments. Memorials include those to the philosopher David Hume (1711-1776), to the Scots who died in the American Civil War, and to the Martyrs of Reform imprisoned or transported for sedition in the 1790s for calling for the right to vote.

stops.name: Dean Bridge
stops.en: is best seen from below in Dean Village as you follow the walkway along the stream - from the top it's just a busy thoroughfare. Crossing in four arches 107 ft / 32 m above the stream, it was Telford's last major project. As well as improving the route to Fife, it made the north bank into prime real estate, so elegant terraces were built there.

stops.name: St Cecilia's Hall
stops.en: Scotland's oldest purpose-built concert hall, opened in 1763 and still in regular use. It hosts the University of Edinburgh collection of historic musical instruments, crafted 16th to 20th century, many of which (such as the Trompette Demilune) are no longer played.

stops.name: St Andrew's and St George's West Church
stops.en: Completed in 1784, this is the parish church of the New Town. It's Italianate with an unusual elliptical interior, with an ornate ceiling blending Roman, Pompeian and Scottish elements. The steeple holds Scotland's oldest complete peal of bells, cast in 1788. In 1843 this church was the scene of The Great Disruption, when a third of ministers broke with the Presbyterian Church of Scotland to found

stops.name: The Georgian House
stops.en: This townhouse was designed by Robert Adam, completed in 1796 and has been furnished in the style of its first owner John Lamont. Its last private owner the Marquess of Bute also acquired adjacent townhouses and along with the other owners got the entire north facade of the square restored to Adams' imposing original design. Visit by self-guided tour, and in mid-summer you need to book as it sells

stops.name: Corstorphine Collegiate Church
stops.en: The present building is a collegiate church of 1429, becoming a parish church in 1646, and re-modeled in 1828.

stops.name: Major General Sir Nils Olav III
Mary King's Close
stops.en: Mary King (1590-1644) was a clothes merchant and city burgess. She died the year before plague struck and carried off the rest of her family. In 1753 Royal Exchange, now City Chambers, was built over several closes by demolishing their upper storeys, while the lower storeys were used for storage then later blocked off. This means a warren of medieval alleys and low dwellings has been preserved, re

stops.name: Writers' Museum
stops.en: This museum, in a tall house built in 1622, celebrates three Scottish literary giants: Robert Burns, Sir Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson. From 1719 the close was the residence of the widow of the 1st Earl of Stair, who ordered the Glencoe massacre.

stops.name: Museum of Edinburgh
stops.en: Museum of city history in a mustard-hued mansion built in 1570.

stops.name: Dean Village
stops.en: It is an attractive hamlet down in the dene - the steep valley - of the Water of Leith. It was the medieval crossing point on the route from Edinburgh to South Queensferry, and is the main access point for this section of the Water of Leith Walkway (described below). The fast-descending stream drove 11 grain mills here, so it was the powerbase for the Baxters, the bakers' merchant guild. The prese

stops.name: Museum of Childhood
stops.en: Concepts and imagery of childhood are ever-changing. See if you can find your (or your grandparents') old toys in the collection, and your place in history.

stops.name: Museum on the Mound
stops.en: Museum about money and coins, in the basement of the Palladian pile of the former Bank of Scotland headquarters. Scotland developed a banking sector in the 18th century to support long-distance trade, and still prints its own banknotes.

stops.name: Charlotte Square
stops.en: In front of the house is the mirror-image of St Andrew's Square at the east end of George St. Bute House at Number 6, next door to The Georgian House, is the official residence of the First Minister of Scotland, so you might see a motorcade, TV cameras and armed security outside. The gardens in the square are private. Prince Albert stands in the middle, with his view down the street somewhat imped

stops.name: People's Story Museum
stops.en: This is housed in Canongate Tolbooth, the medieval centre for governance and justice (preferably gruesome) as Canongate was a separate jurisdiction until 1856. The museum covers the story of working class life, and of organised labour, from the late 18th century to the present.

stops.name: Talbot Rice Gallery
stops.en: David Talbot Rice (1903-72) was in the louche crowd at Oxford that inspired Brideshead Revisited and became a distinguished scholar of East Mediterranean and Russian art, with extensive contacts in those parts - how come this fellow was never implicated in a spy ring? His spell as University Vice Principal is commemorated in this gallery with changing exhibitions of contemporary art. It's housed w

stops.name: City Art Centre
stops.en: Four-floor gallery run by the city council. They rotate artwork from their extensive Scottish collection and have changing exhibitions.

stops.name: Fruitmarket Gallery
stops.en: Gallery of contemporary art, refurbished in 2018. From 1936 to the 1970s this was where soft fruit and veg were traded, handy for the trains and delivery vans.

stops.name: Dynamic Earth
stops.en: Interactive natural history museum exhibiting the forces and features of our planet: volcanoes, polar ice, rainforests and so on. Opened in 1999, it's a tent-like structure on the former site of a gasworks and brewery.

stops.name: Dunbar’s Close Garden
stops.en: This close was re-modelled in the 1970s to recreate a 17th-century physic and knot garden, a hidden quiet place in the busy city.

stops.name: Dovecot Studios
stops.en: Tapestry studio and gallery housed in the former public baths. There is a cafe, shop, and viewing gallery where you can look down on weavers at work.

stops.name: Edinburgh Printmakers
stops.en: Creative centre for printmaking & visual arts, Two free galleries & shop. Vegan Cafe.

stops.name: Greyfriars Kirk
stops.en: This church was built in 1620 on the grounds of an abandoned Franciscan Friary, but seriously damaged by later calamities or Acts of God so the present structure is mostly Victorian. It remains active, as other Presbyterian churches have closed and their congregations moved here. The main visitor interest is the ancient graveyard: notable denizens include the architects William and John Adam, the

stops.name: Anatomical Museum
stops.en: Large collection of anatomical specimens and life and death masks. Best known is the skeleton of William Burke, hanged in 1829 after he and William Hare killed at least 16 people to sell the bodies for dissection. Limited opening as the area is in continual use for teaching, booking essential.

stops.name: Stills
stops.en: Photography gallery with three exhibitions a year. They also support photographers through courses and hire of equipment, darkroom and digital lab.

stops.name: Palestine Museum
stops.en: A branch of their main museum in Woodbridge Connecticut, this is mostly artwork with exhibitions on the Nakhba and other events.

stops.name: Gilbert the Phone Box
stops.en: An old red phone box has been kitted out with Edwardian memorabilia, and nicknamed for Sir Giles Gilbert Scott (1880-1960) designer of the box. You can look in the windows anytime, or collect the key for £3 (for Save the Children) from Stewart Christie and Co who run a long established gentleman's outfitter in the shop next to it.

stops.name: James Clerk Maxwell's Birthplace
stops.en: Isaac Newton realised that what caused the apple to fall was the very same force moving the moon, planets and stars. James Clerk Maxwell (1831-1879) was born in this house, before the family moved to Kirkcudbright. He was intensely curious about how nature worked and made a "great unification" of equal importance to Newton's: that magnetism, electricity, light and heat are all manifestations of th

stops.name: Sherlock Holmes
stops.en: His creator Sir Arthur Conan Doyle (1859-1930) was born nearby at 11 Picardy Place, to a genteel but impoverished Irish Catholic family. His first Sherlock story was published in 1886. The statue was in storage while the plaza was remodelled around the tramlines but restored in June 2023.

stops.name: Patriothall Gallery
stops.en: Small art gallery and artists studios in the former co-op bakery. The gallery has regular exhibitions of modern art. The studios are open.on one weekend in mid-August and another in late November.

stops.name: Museum of Scottish Fire Heritage
stops.en: Volunteer-run museum within McDonald Road fire station. History of Scottish firefighting from the era of rival commercial fire companies, through early wooden fire engines to more recent appliances.

stops.name: Trinity House
stops.en: Stately neo-classical building of 1818 which is now a maritime museum, but only open for special events. It's built over its predecessor of 1560, which in turn was built over a medieval monastic site. The organisation dates back to 1380, when Leith mariners gained the right to levy duty on goods landed at the port; the funds supported sick or aged mariners or their families. They went on to fund l

stops.name: Dr Neil's Garden
stops.en: Secluded terraced garden on the shores of the loch, behind the church. The Neils were a GP couple who laid out the garden in the 1960s. The little tower, built 1825, is not to ward off body-snatchers but a storage space for the heavy curling stones.

stops.name: Upright Gallery
stops.en: Small gallery of local artists' work.

eats.name: The Piemaker
eats.note: This has a wide range of delicious pies and savoury pastries, piping hot. They're mostly a takeaway and don't deliver, but have a few seats inside.

eats.name: Kebab Mahal
eats.note: Good halal curries, kebabs and tandooris, no alcohol.

eats.name: The Original Mosque Kitchen
eats.note: Inexpensive chicken or vegetable curry. A favorite with generations of Edinburgh University students for its cost and portion sizes.

eats.name: Tempting Tattie
eats.note: Inexpensive takeaway for trad baked potatoes.

eats.name: Kampong Ah Lee
eats.note: Tasty Malaysian dishes such as Roti Canai, Satay, Nasi Lemak, Laksa and Rendang.

eats.name: Em’s Kitchen
eats.note: Full Scottish breakfast, shakshuka, coffee and tea options, with seating that looks into a quiet car park and garden.

eats.name: John's Coffee House & Tavern
eats.note: Located in a historic building. Breakfast, all-day waffles, light lunch options, small plates to share, bar with wide range of Scotch whiskies.

eats.name: The Everest
eats.note: Good inexpensive Nepalese and Indian food.

eats.name: Petit Paris
eats.note: Traditional French restaurant complete with chequered tablecloths and whitewashed walls.

eats.name: David Bann
eats.note: Imaginative and tasty vegetarian food, with lots available for vegans or GF.

eats.name: Whiski
eats.note: A bit touristy, but a good choice for Scottish food, drink and music. Hundreds of whiskies available, bar staff happy to advise. Live music every night from 9:30PM, try to sit up front for this.

eats.name: Nok's Kitchen
eats.note: Decent Thai food with vegetarian options. They add 10% service to the menu prices.

eats.name: Kanpai Sushi
eats.note: Small portions of sushi and other Japanese food, and pricey, but speedy service and memorable quality.

eats.name: Gurkha
eats.note: Traditional Indian and Nepalese restaurant.

eats.name: Kalpana
eats.note: Long-established quality vegetarian Indian restaurant serving curries, thalis and tandooris.

eats.name: Tanjore
eats.note: One of the few places in Edinburgh serving South Indian food such as Dosas, Uttapams, Sambar and other Tamil specialities.

eats.name: The Elephant House
eats.note: Consistently good coffee and light bites, cafe is full of university and creative types; JK Rowling wrote much of the first Harry Potter book here. And that alas is the problem: it's become part of th

eats.name: The Witchery by the Castle
eats.note: By the castle entrance, The Witchery serves top-class food in an elegant candle-lit restaurant. They've now added rooms, flamboyantly camp.

eats.name: Timberyard
eats.note: Outstanding Scottish cuisine in a 19th century warehouse, with extensive wine list. One Michelin star, the head chef is Jimmy Murray.

eats.name: The Jolly Judge
eats.note: Cosy independent pub with a good selection of beer and whisky. One of the few pubs on Royal Mile that's not a tourist trap.

eats.name: Albanach
eats.note: Cosy Belhaven pub with food and whisky.

eats.name: Doctors
eats.note: Now a Belhaven pub, this is a welcoming place with good ales and food. It was a few yards from the former Royal Infirmary, within bleep range and sprinting distance for the junior doctors.

eats.name: Sandy Bells
eats.note: Likewise frequented by medical students, this has live folk music every night.

eats.name: The Pear Tree
eats.note: Popular with students, this has a large beer garden and outdoor big screen for TV sports.

eats.name: The Kilderkin
eats.note: Fair selection of cask ales and whisky, the food is so-so and the warmth of welcome varies. This is the original of a chain that now includes The Windsor on Elm Row, Blue Blazer on Spittal St and Benn

eats.name: The Bow Bar
eats.note: Old-style boozer with a large selection of whiskies, selection of guest ales, and no background music.

eats.name: Bennets Bar
eats.note: A good old-fashioned pub, now part of Kilderkin group, with a wide selection of real ale and whisky. It is traditionally the place for pre / post-theatre drinks, with the Kings Theatre.

eats.name: The Bongo Club
eats.note: A café-bar and live music venue.

eats.name: Cabaret Voltaire
eats.note: Atmospheric basement vault with regular gigs.

eats.name: Dragonfly
eats.note: Well-hidden but popular cocktail lounge.

eats.name: The Jazz Bar
eats.note: Live music every night, majoring on jazz; early shows are generally free, later gigs individually priced. Limited food or seating.

eats.name: The Liquid Room
eats.note: 800-capacity live music venue.

eats.name: Wash Bar
eats.note: Modern pub, mostly a local crowd, TV sport, no food.

eats.name: 56 North
eats.note: Cocktail bar incorporating South Loch gin distillery.

eats.name: Snax
eats.note: A small fast-food joint, limited seating. The food is cheap and edible, with a decent vegetarian selection.

eats.name: Cafe Piccante
eats.note: Unashamed specialists in late-night greasy food, friendly staff and a DJ at weekends. The burgers are a stand-out and deep-fried Mars bars are available for tourists.

eats.name: Cafe Royal
eats.note: Beautifully tiled Victorian palace of a pub, designed in 1862 as a showroom for the latest fixtures and fittings, no dogs. The stylish restaurant serves seafood and other classics.

eats.name: Dishoom
eats.note: Scottish outpost of a small national chain, modelling their interiors on colonial Bombay cafes. The food is made to share, mostly consisting of small plates, with the house chaat, black daal and salli

eats.name: The Dome
eats.note: Bar and grill in a former bank headquarters with grand exterior and impressive interior.

eats.name: Pizza Pilgrims
eats.note: This Neapolitan-style chain pizzeria opened its Edinburgh outlet in 2025 to much hype. It's good not great.

eats.name: Mussel Inn
eats.note: Seafood restaurant owned by shellfish producers, ingredients direct from the west coast.

eats.name: Dulse
eats.note: This serves excellent Scottish seafood.

eats.name: Teuchters
eats.note: Lively pub serving modern Scottish cuisine at reasonable prices.

eats.name: Café Marlayne
eats.note: Chic cosy French bistro serving up excellent French cuisine.

eats.name: Cafe St Honoré
eats.note: Great continental food and wine. Gluten free and dairy free menus available.

eats.name: Contini
eats.note: Restaurant in a former grand banking hall serving wonderful Italian food.

eats.name: Holy Cow
eats.note: Excellent basement vegan cafe. Home-made food.

eats.name: The Palmerston
eats.note: Chicly decorated restaurant and bakery in a former bank, the menu changes daily.

eats.name: Voodoo Rooms
eats.note: Over-the-top decor in this quirky pub, sometimes has live entertainment, mixed reviews for the food.

eats.name: All Bar One
eats.note: Chain pub with slick service and good ale and meals.

eats.name: Eastside
eats.note: Busy cocktail bar and night entertainment spot.

eats.name: The Standing Order
eats.note: A cavernous converted bank building. It's part of the JD Wetherspoon chain and always has a wide range of inexpensive drinks and pub food.

eats.name: Tonic
eats.note: A great cocktail bar with friendly helpful staff.

eats.name: The Oxford Bar
eats.note: Trad drouthy Scottish pub, often a setting in the Ian Rankin "Inspector Rebus" novels.

eats.name: The Kenilworth
eats.note: Splendidly tiled and wood-panelled pub.

eats.name: Mathers
eats.note: Traditional bar with a good range of real ales and whisky, reasonable pub food. Big screen for football and rugby.

eats.name: The Basement
eats.note: Nowadays specialising in Mexico, so this is the place for tequila or tacos.

eats.name: Barony Bar
eats.note: Trad pub, dog-friendly, sometimes has live music. It calls itself a gastropub but customers don't much rate the food.

eats.name: The Cask & Barrel
eats.note: This often features in the novels of Christopher Brookmyre as the pub where journalist "Jack Parlabane" gets tip-offs from the police. The Cask is a proper boozer with a wide selection of Real Ale plu

eats.name: The Cumberland Bar
eats.note: Readers of Alexander McCall Smith's 44 Scotland Street will recognise this literary haunt. It's a traditional pub popular with New Town locals, students, the suits from local offices, pretty much ever

eats.name: Edinburgh Gin Distillery
eats.note: Micro-distillery producing gin in various styles. In summer 2024 they plan to move to larger premises on Market St near the station.

eats.name: The Bailie
eats.note: Lovely old trad basement pub, known as much for its ale as its food. Standard pub-grub menu, but quality and prices are a notch higher.

eats.name: Avery
eats.note: Innovative Scots fare in a restaurant with one Michelin Star.

eats.name: The Raeburn
eats.note: Restaurant, pub, beer garden and small hotel in a house built in 1832.

eats.name: Scran and Scallie
eats.note: Upmarket gastro pub with modern Scots cuisine, slick service. They also run the Michelin-starred Kitchin in Leith.

eats.name: Eòrna
eats.note: Rave reviews for their Scottish fine dining. The name means "barley".

eats.name: The Orchard
eats.note: Friendly pub with bar meals, including gluten free.

eats.name: Mimi's Bakehouse
eats.note: Stockbridge branch of an Edinburgh chain of cafés, serving a fairly standard range of sandwiches, but interesting seasonal cakes and bakes.

eats.name: Little Parlour
eats.note: About 30 flavours of ice cream from Stewart Tower in Perthshire, and a selection of confectionery. The shop was opened as a Gentemen's Hairdressers in 1896 and continued as a barbers until 2024; the s

eats.name: The Stockbridge Tap
eats.note: Trad bar with a good range of ales and whiskies, and a limited food selection.

eats.name: Word of Mouth Bistro
eats.note: Pleasant small bistro for breakfast or lunch. They have another branch in Morningside.

eats.name: Fishers
eats.note: Quality seafood restaurant in an old watchtower.

eats.name: The Ship on The Shore
eats.note: This smart slick place on the waterfront does excellent seafood.

eats.name: The Kings Wark
eats.note: Waterside tavern founded in 1434 serving good modern cuisine.

eats.name: Domenico's
eats.note: Friendly small trattoria by the harbour.

eats.name: The Roseleaf
eats.note: Friendly relaxed cafe bistro.

eats.name: Old Chain Pier
eats.note: A waterfront bistro.

eats.name: Little Chartroom
eats.note: Bistro with quality Scots cuisine.

eats.name: Ardfern
eats.note: Splendid little licensed cafe.

eats.name: Cilantro
eats.note: Great reviews for this small Indian and Bangladeshi restaurant. BYOB from Sainsbury's opposite.

eats.name: Restaurant Martin Wishart
eats.note: Leith's first Michelin Star, serving very good food especially the tasting menu, but several found it short of the "outstanding" implied by the Star.

eats.name: Heron
eats.note: Another outstanding restaurant, try the tasting menu.

eats.name: Dogstar
eats.note: This opened in 2026 and quickly drew great reviews for its modern Scottish cuisine.

eats.name: Teuchters Landing
eats.note: Friendly pub with food in a former cruise liner waiting room. Lots of outside tables by the water so a great choice for a sunny afternoon. They have another branch in the West End.

eats.name: Nobles
eats.note: Elegantly decorated cafe bar with good food. Run by the local Bellfield brewery.

eats.name: Nauticus
eats.note: Nautical-themed pub with dark panelling, they have beer but are mainly a whisky and cocktail bar. No food.

eats.name: Starbank Inn
eats.note: Fine real ales with a view over the Firth of Forth. Food available.

eats.name: Port of Leith Distillery
eats.note: This converted biscuit factory is a vertical distillery - water is pumped just once up the nine-storey building and gravity does the rest, more efficient than multiple intermediate pumping. There's a

eats.name: Lind and Lime Distillery
eats.note: They make gin, named for James Lind the Scottish surgeon who advocated the use of limes to treat and prevent scurvy at sea. In 1747 he conducted the world's first controlled clinical trial, comparing

eats.name: The Bonnington
eats.note: Friendly neighbourhood pub with bar food (kitchen closes 9PM).

eats.name: Old Eastway Tap
eats.note: Excellent dog-friendly pub with knowledgeable staff.

eats.name: Scotch Malt Whisky Society
eats.note: Connoisseur whisky-drinkers' private club, with other branches on Queen St and in Glasgow, trying to convey old-money opulence and exclusivity without snootiness and froideur. If you've genuinely got

eats.name: Bonoful
eats.note: Reliable place for Indian food.

eats.name: Foresters Guild
eats.note: Good pub fare and cask ales, inside or in one of their beach huts.

eats.name: Malvarosa
eats.note: Good selection of tapas and slick service.

eats.name: The Beach House
eats.note: Right by the beach with sea views, good selection of food.

eats.name: Mouse Hole Deli
eats.note: Good value deli for takeaway food.

eats.name: Cherry's Cafe
eats.note: A small cafe serving Turkish food and breakfast.

eats.name: Sheep Heid Inn
eats.note: 18th-century pub, with implausible claims to date from 1360, and perhaps named for the village slaughter-ground. In 1745 Bonnie Prince Charlie's army camped outside for a month and he held a Council o

eats.name: The Regent
eats.note: LGBT+ and straight-friendly bar with real ale.

eats.name: The Wee Boulangerie
eats.note: Delicious French bakery for breads, croissants, baguettes and so on. Mostly takeaway but they have a few tables to sit in.

eats.name: Chaskaa
eats.note: Modern Indian restaurant, consistently high quality.

eats.name: Hendersons
eats.note: Renowned vegetarian restaurant, run by the family of the original Hendersons in Hanover St which was open from 1962-2020. Michelin gives it an entry in their guide.

eats.name: LeftField
eats.note: This cosy seafood bistro gets great reviews.

eats.name: Three Birds
eats.note: Fine dining with a classic British menu, but almost entirely GF and much is vegan.

eats.name: The Clay Oven
eats.note: Takeaway offering trad Indian cuisine, fully halal.

eats.name: Bakery Andante
eats.note: Small bakery chain with three other city outlets.

eats.name: Hermitage Bar
eats.note: This pub has very good food at reasonable prices and a pleasant modern interior.

eats.name: Voujon
eats.note: Reliable North Indian / Bangladeshi restaurant.

eats.name: Leslie's Bar
eats.note: A trad pub with charming 1890s interior, dog-friendly, changing guest ales and a decent selection of whiskies.

eats.name: Golf Tavern
eats.note: Good food and an outside seating area facing Bruntsfield Links. You can hire golf clubs and balls here to play on the Links.

eats.name: Canny Man's
eats.note: Famously idiosyncratic pub with quirky decor, excellent range of ales, impressive choice of wine and whisky, and decent food.

eats.name: Holyrood Distillery
eats.note: Small distillery making whisky, vodka, gin and rum. Established in 2019, their first whisky went on sale in 2023.

eats.name: First Coast
eats.note: Long-standing bistro serving quality Scots cuisine.

eats.name: Masti
eats.note: Classic North Indian Balti menu.

eats.name: Miller & Carter Cramond Brig
eats.note: Popular chain steakhouse getting great reviews. The old Cramond Brig is now a footbridge over River Almond, follow the east bank for the village and island, and the west bank to hike to South Queensfe

eats.name: Holy Cow Lounge
eats.note: Vegan cafe in Edinburgh Printmakers building.

eats.name: The Murrayfield
eats.note: Friendly pub close to Murrayfield Stadium with screens for TV sport. Decent all-day pub grub.

eats.name: Cramond Inn
eats.note: Traditional village pub run by Samuel Smiths. Beer garden outside but food service is indoors-only. No dogs.
